scenes.narration: Lists can change. Sometimes you want a collection that cannot. Today we meet the tuple.

scenes.onScreen: "A fixed list": three numbered lines (1. A tuple uses round brackets; 2. It can be read like a list but never changed; 3. Unpacking ties each item to its own name) and an analogy card: a sealed envelope with a fixed set of papers inside: you can read them, but you cannot swap one
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A tuple is like a list that cannot change. It uses round brackets. You can read items by index, count them with len, and loop over them. But you cannot assign to an item, append, or remove. Think of a sealed envelope. You can read the papers, but you cannot swap one. Unpacking is a neat trick. Write several names on the left, and Python ties one item to each name.

scenes.narration: Here is the picture. Spot is tied to a tuple object holding fifteen and seventy three. Lat and lon are tied to the same two int objects that sit inside the tuple. Unpacking did not copy the numbers. It just tied a new name to each one. The tuple itself can never change.

scenes.narration: [HL 1] A tuple of three marks. [HL 2] Unpack into three names. Low, mid and high. [HL 3] Print the first and the last. Seventy two, ninety. [HL 4] A star in front of a name means, collect whatever is left, into a list. First gets seventy two. Rest gets eighty five and ninety. [HL 5] Print both. The rest is a list.

low, mid, high = marks
print(low, high)

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: changing a tuple item
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We try to change the first number of the tuple. Python says, type error. A tuple object does not support item assignment. Tuples are sealed. If you need a different tuple, build a new one, and tie the name to it. If you need to change items often, use a list instead.

shorts.title: What is a tuple?
shorts.hook: "A tuple is like a list that cannot change."
shorts.script: A tuple is like a list that cannot change. It uses round brackets. You can read items by index, count them with len, and loop over them. But you cannot assign to an item, or append, or remove. Use a tuple when the values belong together and should never change, like a latitude and longitude. It tells every reader, this is fixed. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A list that is sealed.

shorts.title: Unpacking
shorts.script: Unpacking is a lovely trick. Write several names on the left, and a tuple on the right. Python ties the first name to the first item. It ties the second name to the second item, and continues like this. Lat, comma, lon, equals spot. Two names, two values, one line. The number of names must match the number of items, or Python raises an error. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Many names, one line.

shorts.title: The star name
shorts.hook: "A star in front of a name means, collect everything that is left."
shorts.script: A star in front of a name means, collect everything that is left. First, comma, star rest, equals a tuple of three marks. First gets the first mark. Rest gets a list of the others. This is useful when you only care about the head of a collection, and want the tail as a bundle. It works with lists too. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Collect the leftovers.

shorts.title: Tuples are sealed
shorts.script: Here is the bug. You try to change one item of a tuple. Spot, bracket zero, equals twenty. Python says, type error, tuple object does not support item assignment. Tuples are immutable. They are sealed on purpose. Build a new tuple if you need different values. Or use a list, if the values must change often. Pick the right tool. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Sealed on purpose.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.hook: "Why did the tuple refuse to change?"
shorts.script: Why did the tuple refuse to change? It was already set in its ways. Your challenge. Make a tuple called rgb, holding two fifty five, one twenty eight, and zero. Unpack it into three names, r, g and b. Then print the three names on one line. You should see the three numbers, in order. Post your code in the comments. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 29.
